outcome: I can describe a person or thing with a correctly matched adjective.
explanation: An adjective describes a noun. It usually matches that noun's grammatical gender and number: petit, petite, petits, petites mean small. Many adjectives follow the noun; some common ones, such as petit and grand (big/tall), usually precede it. Colour words normally follow: une porte bleue means a blue door. Nationality adjectives use lower-case letters: française means French, feminine singular. Some colour expressions, such as bleu clair (light blue), do not change form.

outcome: I can say that an action does not happen, never happens or no longer happens.
explanation: A negative sentence denies something. In careful written French, put ne before the changed verb and pas after it: je ne parle pas means I do not speak. Ne becomes n' before a vowel sound. Replace pas with jamais for never or plus for no longer. In everyday speech people often drop ne, but practise both parts in writing. A short non means no; pas encore means not yet. After a negative quantity statement, un/une/des often becomes de: je n'ai pas de livre means I have no book.

outcome: I can ask a simple yes/no question and request basic information.
explanation: A statement can become a spoken question when your voice rises at the end: tu viens ? means are you coming? Est-ce que also introduces a yes/no question without changing normal subject order. Question words ask for missing information: où (where), quand (when), comment (how), pourquoi (why), combien (how much/many). Inversion means placing a verb before its subject word, joined by a hyphen: venez-vous ? is a more formal are you coming? An inserted t in parle-t-il ? helps pronunciation.

outcome: I can read and give basic time, weather and everyday information.
explanation: Learn vocabulary inside useful messages. Il est introduces clock time: il est neuf heures means it is nine o'clock. A date uses le plus a number and a month: le deux mai means May second; use le premier for the first. Months and weekdays are lower-case. Il fait froid means it is cold; il pleut means it is raining. Ma sœur means my sister; un magasin is a shop; du pain is some bread. French prices use euros, and numbers often use a decimal comma in writing.

outcome: I can describe a daily routine and say how often I do an activity.
explanation: A routine describes repeated actions. A reflexive verb uses a small word pointing back to the person acting: je me lève means I get up; nous nous levons means we get up. The extra word changes with the person: me, te, se, nous, vous, se. Before a vowel, me becomes m'. Souvent means often, toujours means always and parfois means sometimes. Use aimer plus an unchanged verb for preferences: j'aime lire means I like reading.

outcome: I can locate a person or thing and connect two simple ideas.
explanation: A preposition is a small linking word that shows a relationship. À often locates someone in a city; de can show origin or possession; chez means at someone's home or workplace. En is used with many feminine country names, such as en France. Il y a means there is or there are. The words à gauche and à droite mean on the left and on the right. Et (and), mais (but) and parce que (because) connect short ideas. Learn the whole phrase because English and French prepositions do not always match.

(how much does it cost?). To describe a near-future plan, use the present form of aller (to go) followed by an unchanged action word: je vais manger means I am going to eat. This pattern is called futur proche. Read the model aloud as a customer, then answer as the server; reading aloud supports speaking but is not a recorded listening assessment.
feedback.error: The response does not match the model wording requested for: Hello, I would like a coffee.
feedback.remediation: Compare the subject, verb form, spelling and punctuation with: Bonjour, je voudrais un café.
